title: Category codes treated as quantities: the fix, and what each encoding is really worth (DCLAB-R11)
request: The feature recipes took logs and ratios of factorized category codes. Keep the codes out of derived features, then treat them as categories inside training folds, and measure on identical training folds, never the holdout, whether a proper encoding recovers the lift that arithmetic on codes appeared to give.
spec: dclab_rnd/categoricals.py resolves which numeric columns are codes (the catalog's declarations win; a heuristic of whole numbers with at most 20 distinct values applies only without one). FeatureEngineer, the expansion recipes, the DCLab notebook and its exported notebook keep codes out of derived features; the notebook one-hot encodes them with fit-fold levels; a new campaign category_codes_v1 measures legacy, numbers, one-hot and native LightGBM categorical splits with fold-paired, Nadeau-Bengio corrected 95% intervals; existing results untouched.
plan: Read the categorical declarations already kept per dataset in the agentic catalog and resolve code columns from them, with the heuristic as fallback.
Keep codes out of every derived feature in FeatureEngineer, the expansion recipes and the notebook; fix them once per project on training rows and record them.
Re-check informally on identical training folds that the old behaviour reproduces EXP-008 and EXP-028, and see what removing code arithmetic costs.
One-hot encode codes in the notebook's encoder with levels learned on each fit fold (top 40, unseen levels all zero) and route them to the one-hot branch in the exported notebook.
Write category_codes_v1: CAT-001 (playbook ladder, 3x3 repeated folds whose first repeat is the campaign's own), CAT-002 (the notebook's recipes and folds).
Add CAT-003 and CAT-004 for native LightGBM categorical splits on the same folds, with one sensitivity variant declared before any native result.
List the affected old records in evidence/README.md; regenerate the index, SFT and research indexes; run rd-check.

decisions.why: The heuristic misses codes with more levels (native-country, day_of_week) and would misread letter recognition's integer shape statistics as codes.

decisions.decision: FeatureEngineer keeps codes as numbers by default and gains an opt-in one_hot_codes flag, not a new ladder stage.
decisions.why: Encoding is orthogonal to the derivation rungs; changing raw would change every model_building_50_v1 rerun (CAT-001 shows the current code reproduces them exactly); and the ladder's LightGBM gains nothing measurable from it.

decisions.decision: Records made before the change export with codes as numbers.
decisions.why: The exported notebook must reproduce exactly what the engine evaluated then.

decisions.decision: Keep one-hot in the notebook after the native test.
decisions.why: For LightGBM no encoding was distinguishable at this data size, and one-hot is the rule-compliant one that pays for linear models.

decisions.decision: Declare min_data_per_group = 20 as the only native variant, before seeing any native result.
decisions.why: LightGBM's default of 100 is large next to 800 to 3,200 training rows; varying more settings after seeing results would be tuning on the comparison.

change: New dclab_rnd/categoricals.py; FeatureEngineer takes categorical and one_hot_codes; DatasetSpec.categorical_columns and recipes skip codes; the notebook's encoder one-hot encodes codes per fit fold and the feature record says how; the exported notebook routes CATEGORY_CODES to the one-hot branch (cast to text) and old records export unchanged; new dclab_rnd/code_encoding.py and evidence/campaigns/category_codes_v1 (CAT-001 to CAT-004); tests/test_category_codes.py.

findings.defect: The feature recipes did arithmetic on factorized category codes.
findings.scenario: bank_marketing stores month as codes in order of first appearance (May=0, Jun=1, ...); the logs recipe built log1p_month, ratios divided by month and job, and interactions, KMeans and quantile bins used codes. EXP-010's top features were poutcome, log1p_poutcome, month and log1p_month. Found while building the product demo, where log1p_month showed among the top features.
findings.cause: The cached UCI tables were factorized by an earlier downloader, and FeatureEngineer treated every numeric column as a quantity.
findings.fix: Resolve code columns from the catalog's declarations (heuristic as fallback) and keep them out of every derived feature in the ladder, the expansion recipes, the notebook and its export.
findings.impact: Models on bank_marketing and german_credit were scored with features such as log1p_month, where the log of May=0 and Jun=1 says nothing about months. The campaign selected derived recipes on those features, the product demo showed log1p_month among the top features, and anyone following the records would rebuild the same meaningless features.
alternatives: Resolve codes by the heuristic alone (whole numbers, at most 20 distinct values): set aside because it misses codes with more levels, such as native-country and day_of_week, and would misread letter recognition's integer shape statistics as codes.
Edit the agentic catalog itself: set aside; categoricals.py reads the catalog and leaves it untouched, so recorded agentic recipes stay replayable.
findings.open: Uploaded tables without a declaration still rely on the heuristic, so a code column with more than 20 levels in a user's table is still treated as a quantity.

findings.defect: After the first fix, codes still reached every model as plain numbers.
findings.scenario: The notebook's encoder passed numeric columns through and one-hot encoded only text dtypes, and the exported notebook put code columns in the scaled numeric branch, so a linear model still treated a higher month code as more of a quantity, against DCLAB-R11 ('do not treat arbitrary category codes as ordinal').
findings.cause: Encoding was chosen by dtype, not by meaning.
findings.fix: One-hot encode the resolved code columns with levels learned on each fit fold (the 40 most frequent, unseen levels all zero) and route them to the one-hot branch in the export.
findings.test: Tests show a code column one-hot encoded with fit-fold levels in every recipe and fold, and never in the export's scaled numeric branch.
findings.impact: A linear model read a higher month code as more of something, against DCLAB-R11, on every notebook run with codes. It also cost linear models real signal: one-hot encoding later raised logistic regression by +0.038 on bank_marketing and +0.040 on adult.
alternatives: A new one-hot stage in the feature ladder: set aside for an opt-in one_hot_codes flag, because encoding composes with every derivation rung and changing raw would change every model_building_50_v1 rerun.

Native LightGBM categorical splits: measured afterwards (CAT-003, CAT-004) and set aside; they could not be told apart from one-hot at this data size and collapsed on heart_disease at default settings.
findings.open: A column with more than 40 levels is encoded slightly differently in the engine and in the export: sklearn's max_categories=40 keeps 39 levels plus an 'infrequent' column, while the engine keeps 40. Truly ordered codes (repayment delays, education levels) lose their order under one-hot.

findings.defect: Some conclusions in the campaign's claims were written as fixed sentences, not derived from the intervals.
findings.scenario: Dry-running the claim code on the two smallest datasets showed sentences whose conclusion was fixed text rather than read from the interval, so a claim could say 'within noise' whatever the numbers were.
findings.cause: Claim text drafted from the expected result.
findings.fix: Make every claim conditional on its interval (better, worse or within noise), add a test for the paired-interval helper, and rerun the campaign into its result files.
findings.test: The paired-interval helper test in tests/test_category_codes.py.
findings.impact: The campaign's claims feed the evidence index and the SFT data. A fixed sentence could have said 'within noise' or 'better' whatever the interval showed, so a reader, and a model trained on the claims, would learn a conclusion the numbers did not support.

findings.defect: LightGBM reads negative category values as missing.
findings.scenario: credit_default's PAY codes run from -2; passed directly as categorical_feature, every -2 and -1 would have been treated as missing in the native-split arm.
findings.cause: LightGBM's categorical input must be non-negative integer ids.
findings.fix: Recode codes to category ids learned on each fit fold before passing them; missing and unseen levels get ids of their own.
findings.test: A test checks the model splits a code only by membership (==), never by a threshold.
findings.impact: In the native-split arm every -2 and -1 PAY code of credit_default would have become 'missing', merging distinct repayment states into one. Native splits would then have been judged on damaged input and possibly rejected for the wrong reason.
alternatives: Pass the codes to categorical_feature as they are: set aside because LightGBM's categorical input must be non-negative integer ids.

findings.defect: The selected_mi recipe got worse under one-hot encoding.
findings.scenario: selected_mi keeps 60% of the input columns, counted before encoding, but now picks among the encoded columns, so it keeps fewer inputs: bank_marketing -0.0411, german_credit -0.0184 under one-hot vs numbers.
findings.cause: Its k is sized on input columns, not encoded ones.
findings.fix: Not changed here: recorded as a risk in CAT-002 (the rule selected it on no dataset with one-hot codes); sizing k on encoded columns is a separate change.
findings.impact: Under one-hot codes, selected_mi keeps 60% of a column count taken before encoding, so it keeps fewer real inputs. Its scores understate one-hot on bank_marketing and german_credit, and a project whose rule picked it would get a weaker model.
findings.open: k is still sized on input columns; until it is sized on encoded columns, selected_mi is handicapped whenever codes are one-hot encoded.

findings.defect: Native LightGBM categorical splits collapse on a small dataset at default settings.
findings.scenario: On heart_disease (about 240 training rows) native splits at defaults lost 0.053 ROC-AUC on the ladder folds and 0.056 on the notebook folds against codes as numbers.
findings.cause: min_data_per_group=100 is too large for categories with few rows each.
findings.fix: The pre-declared variant min_data_per_group=20 removes the loss (+0.002 and +0.010); if native splits are ever offered, the setting must scale with the training rows.
findings.impact: On a table of about 240 training rows, native categorical splits at LightGBM's defaults cost about 0.05 ROC-AUC. A user who switched them on for a small table would get a clearly worse model without any error.
alternatives: Tune several LightGBM settings for the native arm: set aside because varying more settings after seeing results would be tuning on the comparison; one variant was declared before any native result.
findings.open: Native splits are not offered. If they ever are, min_data_per_group must scale with the training rows, and the native categorical support of XGBoost and histogram boosting is still untested.

measurements.name: reproduction of the recorded campaign
measurements.gate: On the first repeat's folds the legacy arm must reproduce model_building_50_v1's feature-stage ROC-AUC exactly.
measurements.against_gate: The gate asks for an exact match on the first repeat's folds; the legacy arm matched exactly on 7 of 7 datasets, so it ran the recorded campaign's code on its folds.
limits: Only the first repeat has recorded scores to match; the other repeats are trusted because they come from the same code.
An exact reproduction shows the comparison is fair; it says nothing about whether the recorded lifts were real.

measurements.name: was the derived-recipe lift real
measurements.gate: Legacy derived stage minus raw over 9 folds; real only if the corrected 95% interval excludes zero.
measurements.result: bank_marketing ratios - raw +0.0012 [-0.0185, +0.0209]; german_credit interactions - raw +0.0006 [-0.0296, +0.0308]; all three arms select raw over 9 folds.
measurements.next: Treat the recorded EXP-008 and EXP-028 lifts as 3-fold noise.
measurements.against_gate: bank_marketing ratios minus raw is +0.0012 with an interval from -0.0185 to +0.0209, and german_credit interactions minus raw is +0.0006 from -0.0296 to +0.0308. Both intervals include zero, so neither lift is real by the gate, and all three arms select raw over 9 folds.
limits: The folds are small, so the intervals are wide: an effect of a few thousandths can be neither confirmed nor ruled out.
The Nadeau-Bengio correction approximates the dependence between overlapping training sets; it is not an exact test.
Only bank_marketing and german_credit carried a derived-recipe lift worth checking; the result says nothing about derived recipes on other data.

measurements.name: does one-hot recover the lift
measurements.gate: One-hot raw minus the legacy derived stage, corrected 95% interval above zero.
measurements.result: bank_marketing -0.0065 [-0.0305, +0.0175]; german_credit +0.0178 [-0.0131, +0.0488]. LightGBM one-hot minus numbers within noise on 7 of 7; logistic regression better on bank_marketing (+0.038) and adult (+0.040), and in the notebook on adult (+0.056) and online_shoppers (+0.069); Extra Trees worse on adult, credit_default and online_shoppers (-0.014 to -0.030).
measurements.next: Keep one-hot for rule compliance and linear models; test native splits next.
measurements.against_gate: One-hot raw minus the legacy derived stage is -0.0065 [-0.0305, +0.0175] on bank_marketing and +0.0178 [-0.0131, +0.0488] on german_credit: neither interval lies above zero, so one-hot does not recover the lift. Outside the gate, logistic regression gains +0.038 on bank_marketing and +0.040 on adult, and Extra Trees loses -0.014 to -0.030 on adult, credit_default and online_shoppers.
limits: The lift it tried to recover was itself fold noise, so failing to recover it says little against one-hot.
The gate judges the stage model only; the logistic-regression gains and the Extra Trees losses were not gated.
Training folds only and no holdout read: these are development estimates.

measurements.name: same folds for the native arms
measurements.gate: The numbers arm re-run through each native experiment's loop must match the stored CAT-001 and CAT-002 fold scores exactly.
measurements.next: Compare native fold by fold with the stored arms.
measurements.against_gate: The numbers arm, re-run through each native experiment's own loop, matched the stored fold scores exactly on 14 of 14 dataset runs, as the gate requires.
limits: The match proves identical folds and code for the numbers arm; the native arm's own recoding is covered by a separate test, not by this check.
It makes the comparison fair; it says nothing about which encoding is better.

measurements.name: do native categorical splits beat numbers or one-hot
measurements.gate: Native minus numbers and minus one-hot, corrected 95% intervals; better only if an interval excludes zero above it.
measurements.result: Native minus numbers within noise on 7 of 7 in both pipelines (means -0.007 and -0.010); native minus one-hot within noise except german_credit on the ladder (-0.022 [-0.034, -0.010]); min_data_per_group=20 within noise everywhere (means +0.002 and +0.001); native raw vs the recorded derived stages: bank_marketing +0.010 [-0.031, +0.050], german_credit -0.004 [-0.029, +0.021].
measurements.next: Keep one-hot in the notebook; XGBoost and histogram boosting's native support remain untested, and truly ordered codes (repayment delays, education levels) lose their order under both one-hot and native splits.
measurements.against_gate: Native minus numbers stays within noise on 7 of 7 datasets in both pipelines (means -0.007 and -0.010). Native minus one-hot excludes zero only on german_credit on the ladder, and there on the losing side (-0.022 [-0.034, -0.010]). The declared min_data_per_group=20 variant is within noise everywhere (means +0.002 and +0.001). No interval lies above zero, so native splits are not better by the gate.
limits: Only LightGBM was tested; XGBoost and histogram boosting have native categorical support of their own.
One sensitivity variant was declared; other settings could behave differently, and trying them now would be tuning on the comparison.
At this data size the intervals are wide enough to hide a small real gain.
Codes with a true order lose it under both one-hot and native splits, so neither arm tests an ordered encoding.

outcome: Codes are now kept out of derived features and one-hot encoded inside folds in the DCLab notebook, matching DCLAB-R11. The measurement overturned the idea behind the task: the code-arithmetic lift was 3-fold noise, and for LightGBM at this data size numbers, one-hot and native splits cannot be told apart. Old results stay as recorded, with the affected records listed.
lessons: Before fixing a feature to recover a lift, check the lift is real on more folds; here it was noise.
Prove two arms ran on the same folds by reproducing a stored score exactly, not by assuming it.
Declare a sensitivity variant before seeing results, and only one.
A rule-compliant encoding can be worth keeping even when it does not raise the score.
risks: Fixing the encoding to recover a lift that was never real, because the original lift was measured on only a few folds.
Resolving code columns by a heuristic that misses codes with many levels or mistakes integer measurements for codes.
Changing FeatureEngineer's defaults and so breaking the exact reproduction of every recorded campaign result.
Comparing encodings on folds that differ, so a difference reflects the split rather than the encoding.
Passing codes straight to LightGBM's native categorical input, where negative values are read as missing.
